program_overview.title: Informatik Abitur in English: Java and Python
program_overview.tagline: Object-oriented programming, data structures, automata, databases and networks for Abitur Informatik, live and in English, with a mentor who matches your pace and accent.
program_overview.description:
This is a live online course for students in the gymnasiale Oberstufe in Germany who take Informatik, from the Einführungsphase through the Qualifikationsphase to the written or oral Abitur. It covers the topics that Abitur Informatik commonly examines: object-oriented modelling and programming, algorithms and their running time, linear and tree data structures, databases and SQL, finite automata and formal languages, networks and cryptography. Students work in Java or in Python, whichever their school uses, and Java students can work in BlueJ, which we support.

Classes are live and taught in English only. The mentor matches each student's pace and accent: speaks clearly, slows down on hard ideas, rephrases and checks understanding. For a student whose first language is German, every class is Informatik help and practice in technical English at the same time, which is useful for university, where much of computing is read and written in English. We never teach in German, but our notes list the German term beside the English one (Klassendiagramm and class diagram, Schlange and queue, deterministischer endlicher Automat and deterministic finite automaton), so the work links straight back to school.

The written Abitur in Informatik is often a paper exam. The GI Informatik-Monitor 2026/27 says of Bayern that "Große Teile des schriftlichen Informatikabiturs beinhalten Programmieraufgaben auf Papier, jedoch keine praktischen Anteile am Rechner", and of NRW that "Der Einsatz eines Computers ist für die Bearbeitung der schriftlich Abituraufgaben nicht vorgesehen." So we train both halves: real programs written and tested on a computer, and clean code, diagrams and explanations written by hand under time. The same monitor reports that in the NRW Qualifikationsphase Informatik can be a Grundkurs of three hours or a Leistungskurs of five, and that in Sachsen the Leistungskurs is available at selected Gymnasien only. Topics, weighting and exam rules differ by Land and year, so the mentor maps the course to the student's own Land and course level in the first class. Every practice question and mock paper is our own; we never reproduce real Abitur tasks. We are independent of every Land ministry and make no promise of grades.
what_makes_this_different: Live classes in English only, with a mentor who matches your pace and accent and slows down whenever a topic is hard
Java or Python, matched to your school, with BlueJ supported for Java classes
Paper-exam training: writing code, class diagrams and automata by hand under time, because written Informatik Abitur papers are often done without a computer
Grundkurs and Leistungskurs paths: the Leistungskurs path adds graphs, pushdown automata and more depth on running time
Mapped to your Land and phase in the first class, because Oberstufe Informatik differs between NRW, Bayern, Sachsen and the rest
Original mock papers in the Abitur style every month, never copies of real tasks

learning_path.phase_1: Object-oriented modelling and programming in Java or Python: classes, objects, UML class diagrams, inheritance, arrays, searching, sorting, recursion and running time
learning_path.phase_2: Data structures and databases: lists, stacks, queues, binary trees and graphs, then entity-relationship models, the relational model and SQL
learning_path.phase_3: Theory and systems: finite automata, grammars and formal languages, networks and cryptography, and exam craft with timed papers of our own

career_outcomes: Confident, correct object-oriented code in Java or Python
Data structures and algorithms explained with running time
Databases designed with ER models and queried in SQL
Automata and grammars drawn, tested and explained
Clear written answers and hand-written code for paper exams
Technical English for a computing degree, read and spoken with confidence

phase_1_object_oriented_programming.title: PHASE 1: Object-Oriented Modelling and Programming (Months 1-2, Weeks 1-8)
phase_1_object_oriented_programming.description: The programming core every Oberstufe Informatik course builds on, taught in Java or Python and practised both on screen and on paper.

month_1_classes_and_algorithms.title: Month 1: Classes, Objects and Basic Algorithms

week_1_2.title: Weeks 1-2: Your Oberstufe, Your Language, and Objects
topics: A diagnostic: your Land, phase (Einführungsphase or Qualifikationsphase), Grundkurs or Leistungskurs, and school language
How we work in English: the mentor's pace, phrases for asking to repeat, and a German to English term list
Setting up Java with BlueJ, or Python, exactly as your school does
Classes, objects, attributes and methods, and the constructor
UML class diagrams (Klassendiagramme): reading them and drawing them
Encapsulation: private attributes with getter and setter methods
projects: A Konto (bank account) class with deposits, withdrawals and validation, drawn first as a class diagram
week_1_2.practice: Short programs written on screen, then the same code written by hand

week_3_4.title: Weeks 3-4: Control Structures, Arrays, Searching and Sorting
topics: Selection and loops, with trace tables to check them
Arrays (and Python lists): filling, traversing and finding the maximum
Linear search and binary search, and why binary search needs sorted data
Bubble sort, selection sort and insertion sort, traced by hand
Counting comparisons to compare algorithms
Explaining an algorithm in precise English, then in the operator language of exam questions
projects: A sorting comparison program that counts steps for three algorithms
week_3_4.practice: Hand-tracing exercises of our own on searching and sorting
week_3_4.assessment: Month 1 check: a short paper with code to write by hand and a trace table

month_2_oop_and_recursion.title: Month 2: Inheritance, Relationships, Recursion and Running Time

week_5_6.title: Weeks 5-6: Inheritance, Polymorphism and Associations
topics: Inheritance: superclass and subclass, and overriding methods
Polymorphism, abstract classes and interfaces
Associations, aggregation and multiplicities in class diagrams
Modelling a real situation as classes: from a text description to a diagram
Working from a given class documentation, the way written exams often provide it
Discussing a design choice out loud in English
projects: A library or school timetable model with a class hierarchy and associations
week_5_6.practice: Modelling tasks of our own: text in, class diagram and code out

week_7_8.title: Weeks 7-8: Recursion, Faster Sorting and Running Time
topics: Recursion: base case, recursive case and the call stack
Recursive algorithms: factorial, power, binary search and the Towers of Hanoi
Merge sort and quicksort, and why they beat simple sorts on large data
Running time with O notation: constant, linear, quadratic and n log n
Best, average and worst case
Leistungskurs depth: proving a recursive method terminates
projects: A timing experiment that sorts growing arrays and plots the running time
week_7_8.practice: Recursion traces and running-time questions of our own
week_7_8.assessment: Phase 1 assessment: a timed paper of original OOP and algorithm questions, written by hand

phase_2_data_structures_and_databases.title: PHASE 2: Data Structures and Databases (Months 3-4, Weeks 9-16)
phase_2_data_structures_and_databases.description: Abstract data types and the relational database model, two topics that recur across Land curricula for Oberstufe Informatik.

month_3_linear_and_tree_structures.title: Month 3: Lists, Stacks, Queues, Trees and Graphs

week_9_10.title: Weeks 9-10: Linear Data Structures
topics: Abstract data types: what a structure does versus how it is built
Stack (Stapel) and queue (Schlange): operations and typical uses
Linked lists built from nodes (Knoten), with insert, delete and search
Using a given List, Stack or Queue class from its documentation
Choosing a structure for a task and justifying the choice
Drawing pointer diagrams by hand
projects: A print-queue and undo-stack simulator built on your own linked list
week_9_10.practice: Written tasks of our own: use a given list class to solve a problem on paper

week_11_12.title: Weeks 11-12: Binary Trees and Graphs
topics: Binary trees: root, leaves, height, and preorder, inorder and postorder traversal
Binary search trees: insert, search and why balance matters
Leistungskurs depth: graphs as adjacency matrix and adjacency list
Depth-first and breadth-first search
Shortest paths with Dijkstra's algorithm, traced by hand
Explaining a traversal step by step in English
projects: A binary search tree word dictionary with all three traversals
week_11_12.practice: Tree and graph tracing exercises of our own
week_11_12.assessment: Month 3 check: a timed set of data-structure questions on paper

week_13_14.title: Weeks 13-14: Entity-Relationship Models and the Relational Model
topics: Entities, attributes and relationships in an ER model (Entity-Relationship-Modell)
Cardinalities 1:1, 1:n and n:m, and resolving n:m relationships
From ER model to tables: primary keys and foreign keys
Anomalies and normalisation to the third normal form
Relational algebra: selection, projection and join
Data protection and why databases need access rules
projects: An ER model and table design for a sports club, normalised step by step
week_13_14.practice: Modelling tasks of our own: a scenario in words, a model on paper

week_15_16.title: Weeks 15-16: SQL Queries
topics: SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY and DISTINCT
Joins across two and three tables
GROUP BY, HAVING and aggregate functions
Nested queries and when to use them
Reading a query and saying in English what it returns
Writing SQL by hand under exam conditions
projects: A school database queried with twenty SQL questions of rising difficulty
week_15_16.practice: SQL query sets of our own, solved on screen and then on paper
week_15_16.assessment: Phase 2 assessment: a timed paper of original data-structure and database questions

phase_3_theory_systems_exam.title: PHASE 3: Automata, Languages, Networks and Exam Craft (Months 5-6, Weeks 17-24)
phase_3_theory_systems_exam.description: Theoretical informatics and computer systems, then a month of exam technique with timed papers of our own.

week_17_18.title: Weeks 17-18: Finite Automata
topics: Alphabets, words and languages
Deterministic finite automata: states, transitions, start and accepting states
Drawing a transition diagram and writing the transition table
Designing an automaton for a given language, and testing it with words
Nondeterministic finite automata and converting them to deterministic ones
Implementing an automaton in Java or Python
projects: A validator for number plates or email-like strings, built as an automaton in code
week_17_18.practice: Automaton design tasks of our own, drawn by hand and tested

week_19_20.title: Weeks 19-20: Grammars, Pushdown Automata and Limits
topics: Regular grammars and regular expressions, and their link to finite automata
Context-free grammars, derivations and syntax trees
Leistungskurs depth: pushdown automata (Kellerautomaten) for nested brackets
Why some languages need more than a finite automaton
An overview of the Turing machine and the limits of computation
Explaining a proof idea clearly in English
projects: A bracket checker built as a pushdown automaton with a stack
week_19_20.practice: Grammar and automaton questions of our own
week_19_20.assessment: Month 5 check: a timed theory paper on automata and grammars

month_6_networks_crypto_exam.title: Month 6: Networks, Cryptography and Abitur Exam Craft

week_21_22.title: Weeks 21-22: Networks and Cryptography
topics: Layer models: the TCP/IP model and the ISO/OSI model
IP addressing, routing, DNS and the client-server model
Protocols as agreed rules, and a simple protocol designed in class
Symmetric encryption: Caesar and Vigenère, and how they are broken
Asymmetric encryption, the idea behind RSA, and digital signatures
Security, privacy and the social side of networks
projects: A Vigenère encoder and cracker, plus a short written explanation of RSA
week_21_22.practice: Network and cryptography scenarios of our own to explain in full sentences

week_23_24.title: Weeks 23-24: Abitur Exam Technique and Mock Papers
topics: The operators in exam questions (nennen, beschreiben, erläutern, implementieren) and what each asks for, explained in English
Writing correct code by hand: layout, naming and checking without a compiler
Timed mock papers of our own in the Abitur style, Grundkurs or Leistungskurs
Oral exam practice: explaining a model or algorithm aloud and answering follow-up questions
An error log review and a personal revision plan up to the exam
Matching the plan to your Land's exam dates and rules
projects: Two full timed mock papers with detailed written feedback
week_23_24.practice: A timed paper of original questions and a spoken explanation
week_23_24.assessment: Final assessment: a full timed paper of original questions and an oral explanation

faqs.question: What does the Informatik Oberstufe and Abitur course cover?
faqs.answer: Object-oriented programming in Java or Python, UML class diagrams, searching, sorting, recursion and running time, lists, stacks, queues, trees and graphs, ER models and SQL, finite automata and formal languages, networks and cryptography, and exam technique. It is a live online course for Oberstufe students in Germany, roughly ages 16 to 19, taught in English.

faqs.question: Are the classes in German or in English?
faqs.answer: English only. We never teach in German. The mentor matches your pace and accent: speaks clearly, slows down on hard topics, rephrases and checks understanding. Many students see this as a plus: you get Informatik help and practice in technical English at once, which helps later at university. Our notes list the German school term beside the English one.

faqs.question: Java or Python?
faqs.answer: Whichever your school uses. Students whose school teaches Java can work in BlueJ, and Python students work in Python. The ideas are the same, and the mentor shows the code in your language.

faqs.question: Is it for Grundkurs or Leistungskurs?
faqs.answer: Both. The Grundkurs path covers the core; the Leistungskurs path adds graphs and shortest paths, pushdown automata and more depth on running time and proof. In NRW, for example, the GI Informatik-Monitor 2026/27 reports a three-hour Grundkurs and a five-hour Leistungskurs in the Qualifikationsphase.

faqs.question: Does the course follow my Land's curriculum?
faqs.answer: It covers the topics that recur across Land curricula, and the mentor maps it to your Land, phase and course level in the first class. Topics and exam rules differ by Land and year, so we check your school's current list with you rather than assume.

faqs.question: Is the written Informatik Abitur done on a computer?
faqs.answer: Often not. The GI Informatik-Monitor 2026/27 says written Abitur tasks in Bayern are largely programming on paper with no work on a computer, and that in NRW a computer is not used for the written tasks. That is why we practise writing code, diagrams and automata by hand under time, as well as programming on screen.

faqs.question: Do you use real Abitur tasks?
faqs.answer: No. Every practice question and mock paper is our own, written in the Abitur style. Students can use the past tasks their Land publishes themselves; we never copy them into our materials.

faqs.question: Can the Bundeswettbewerb Informatik count toward my Abitur?
faqs.answer: Possibly. BWINF says round 2 of the Bundeswettbewerb Informatik can count as the besondere Lernleistung in the Abitur, depending on Land and school. Ask your school. Our German Informatics Competitions course prepares for the Bundeswettbewerb.

faqs.question: When are classes, with the time difference to India?
faqs.answer: Timing is flexible on weekdays or weekends: choose a batch, or 1-on-1 at your convenience. Our teachers work in India time, which is 4 hours 30 minutes ahead of Germany in winter and 3 hours 30 minutes ahead in summer, so German afternoon, early evening and weekend slots are realistic.

faqs.question: Do you promise a grade?
faqs.answer: No. We promise careful teaching, honest feedback and regular timed practice. We are independent of every Land ministry and school, and our certificate is not an Abitur grade or German qualification.

faqs.question: What do I need?
faqs.answer: A computer with stable internet, a headset with a microphone, and Java with BlueJ or Python installed (we help in the first class), plus paper and pen for hand-written practice.

faqs.question: Can I try a class first?
faqs.answer: Yes. The first class is a free demo, so you can hear the mentor's pace and decide with no pressure.
